power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Background & Objectives: As recently recommended by neuropathologists, we assessed the diagnostic accuracy of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) alpha-synuclein (α-syn) seed amplification assay (SAA) in an autopsy cohort with systemic assessment of Lewy pathology.
text.formatted: Background & Objectives: As recently recommended by neuropathologists, we assessed the diagnostic accuracy of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) alpha-synuclein (α-syn) seed amplification assay (SAA) in an autopsy cohort with systemic assessment of Lewy pathology.

text.text: Methods: CSF was obtained antemortem and stored at -80 . α-syn SAA and systemic Lewy pathology assessment were conducted as previously reported.
Kinetic parameters, including maximum fluorescence (F max ) and time to reach 50% of Fmax (T 50 ), were also evaluated.
Results: CSF samples were available from 30 patients (8 with symptomatic Lewy body disease [LBD], 2 with multiple system atrophy [MSA], 3 with Alzheimer's disease [AD], and 17 disease controls).

Despite different clinical stages, all patients with LBD had diffuse neocortical or limbic-stage pathology at autopsy, with widespread peripheral Lewy bodies, including in the esophagus, heart, and sympathetic ganglia.
Lewy pathology was not observed in disease controls.
SAA was positive in all 8 with LBD, "low positive" in one patient with AD, and negative in all others.
F max was significantly higher in LBD compared with cases without α-syn pathology (9091±2083 vs. 1659±113 relative fluorescence units).
The low-positive case had a lower positivity rate (25% vs. 75-100%), lower F max , and longer T 50 than LBD cases.

In this pilot study, CSF α-syn SAA demonstrated high specificity (95%) and high sensitivity (100%) for detecting LBD; however, all LBD cases had widespread pathology, including peripheral involvement.
Larger studies are needed to understand the association between CSF α-syn SAA and Lewy pathology in the body.
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) α-synuclein (α-syn) seed amplification assays (SAA) have been reported to have high sensitivity and specificity for detecting Lewy body disease (LBD) (1) (2) (3) (4) (5).
text.formatted: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) α-synuclein (α-syn) seed amplification assays (SAA) have been reported to have high sensitivity and specificity for detecting Lewy body disease (LBD) <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref>.

text.text: Recently, SAA has been proposed as a method to confirm the presence or absence of Lewy pathology in Parkinson's disease (PD) and to define a new disease entity, namely neuronal α-syn disease (6, 7).
text.formatted: Recently, SAA has been proposed as a method to confirm the presence or absence of Lewy pathology in Parkinson's disease (PD) and to define a new disease entity, namely neuronal α-syn disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">7)</ref>.

text.text: However, previous autopsy validation studies have shown that the sensitivity of α-syn SAA is not optimal when Lewy pathology is limited, such as in the amygdala or brainstem (8) (9) (10) (11).
text.formatted: However, previous autopsy validation studies have shown that the sensitivity of α-syn SAA is not optimal when Lewy pathology is limited, such as in the amygdala or brainstem <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(8)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(9)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(10)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(11)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, we recently proposed that sensitivity in patients with early PD may be affected by peripheral involvement, as reflected by abnormalities on cardiac metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scintigraphy (12).

text.text: Other studies have reported lower SAA sensitivity in patients without hyposmia (13, 14).
text.formatted: Other studies have reported lower SAA sensitivity in patients without hyposmia <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">14)</ref>.

text.text: However, the neuropathological basis for these observations remains unclear.
International neuropathologists have recently highlighted limitations in existing autopsy validation studies of CSF α-syn SAA (11).
text.formatted: International neuropathologists have recently highlighted limitations in existing autopsy validation studies of CSF α-syn SAA <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(11)</ref>.

text.text: Most reported cohorts do not contain the full spectrum of the disease or pathological data in the peripheral organs.
Accordingly, additional community-based studies incorporating full-body autopsy evaluations have been recommended (11).

text.text: Therefore, we conducted a pilot study to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of CSF α-syn SAA in a community-based autopsy cohort with systemic, whole-body assessment of Lewy pathology.

text.text: Briefly, our institution is located in a suburban area of Tokyo, Japan, and provides community-based clinical care for older adults.
CSF biomarker measurements have been conducted for Alzheimer's disease (AD), LBD, and other neurological diseases (15) (16) (17) (18).

text.text: In addition to patients who died in our hospital, individuals who consented to and were registered in the Brain Bank for Aging Research (BBAR) donation program were transferred to our institution for autopsy.
All patients who underwent autopsy and had available CSF samples were included in this study.
This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
Storage of remaining CSF samples for future use was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of the Tokyo Metropolitan Institute for Geriatrics and Gerontology (TMIG).
Written informed consent was obtained from patients or their legal guardians.
The use of clinical and pathological information and remaining CSF samples for this study was approved by the IRB of TMIG (R24-032).
All patients, regardless of clinical diagnosis, underwent a thorough neuropathological evaluation according to the BBAR protocol (20) (21) (22) (23) in accordance with current guidelines.

text.text: Immunostaining was performed using DAB visualization with primary antibodies against phosphorylated α-synuclein (pSyn#64, dilution 1:20,000 with formic acid for antigen retrieval; a gift from T. Iwatsubo, Japan; now commercially available from FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemical Corp., Osaka, Japan).

A systemic Lewy pathology assessment was conducted in all cases, including the olfactory bulb (24), sympathetic ganglia (22, 25), spinal cord (26), and multiple organs in the body, such as the esophagus (23), heart (22, 25), and skin (27).

text.text: α-syn SAA was conducted using the real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) method (32), as previously described (12), with minor modifications.
text.formatted: α-syn SAA was conducted using the real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) method (32), as previously described <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(12)</ref>, with minor modifications.

text.text: Briefly, recombinant α-syn protein (33) was mixed with buffer as previously reported (32) in 96-well plates.
text.formatted: Briefly, recombinant α-syn protein (33) was mixed with buffer as previously reported <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(32)</ref> in 96-well plates.

text.text: Three zirconium/silica beads were added, and reactions were seeded with 5 μL of undiluted CSF to a final reaction volume of 100 μL.

Plates were sealed and incubated in a FLUOstar Omega fluorometer (BMG Labtech, Ortenberg, Germany) at 53 °C for 90 h with intermittent shaking cycles: double orbital shaking for 1 min (400 rpm) followed by 1 min rest.
Thioflavin-T (ThT) fluorescence was measured every 20 min.
Each sample was run in quadruplicate.
The tester was blinded to the clinical and pathological diagnoses.
For the predetermined positivity criteria, a sample was considered positive when ThT fluorescence remained exceeding 2,000 relative fluorescence units (RFU) after 48 h in two or more wells.
If this threshold was exceeded in only one well, the assay was repeated, and the sample was considered "low positive" if one or more wells exceeded the same threshold.
Maximum fluorescence (F max ) and area under the curve (AUC) were calculated for all wells.
Time-to-threshold (TTT) and time to reach 50% of F max (T 50 ) were calculated only for positive wells (34).
text.formatted: Time-to-threshold (TTT) and time to reach 50% of F max (T 50 ) were calculated only for positive wells <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(34)</ref>.

text.text: The positivity rate (positive wells out of four) and mean values of F max , AUC, TTT, and T 50 for each sample were used for further analyses.
All statistical analyses and visualizations were performed using GraphPad Prism version 10 (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, US).
Categorical variables are expressed as percentages.
Normally or non-normally distributed continuous variables are expressed as mean ± standard deviation or median [interquartile range], respectively.
Sensitivity was calculated for patients with symptomatic LBD.
Since previous studies have shown that many assays can detect abnormal α-syn in patients with MSA (2, 34), we excluded patients with MSA in the calculation of specificity.
Specificity was calculated using patients with AD and other disease controls.
For kinetic parameters, after confirming normal distribution, group differences were evaluated using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), followed by Dunnett's post hoc test against normal controls.
Statistical significance was set at P <0.05.
text.formatted: Statistical significance was set at P <0.05.

text.text: Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were conducted for mean F max and mean AUC to discriminate patients with LBD from others (including those with MSA).
The optimal cut-off value was determined using the Youden index.

text.text: CSF samples from 30 patients were analyzed, including 8 with symptomatic LBD, 2 with MSA, 3 with AD, and 17 with other diseases.
Baseline characteristics and disease descriptions are summarized in Table 1.

text.text: Antemortem CSF samples from all eight patients with symptomatic LBD showed positive α-syn SAA results (100% sensitivity).
Details of clinical courses and neuropathological findings are summarized in Figure 1.

text.text: Cardiac MIBG scintigraphy results were available for five patients, and all showed abnormal results.
Despite different clinical stages, autopsy revealed that five patients with symptomatic LBD were in the diffuse neocortical stage and three were in the limbic stage.
All eight patients also showed widespread peripheral LBs, including in the esophagus, heart, and sympathetic ganglia (Figure 1).
text.formatted: All eight patients also showed widespread peripheral LBs, including in the esophagus, heart, and sympathetic ganglia (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Control patients with other diseases showed no peripheral Lewy pathology.
The interval from lumbar puncture to autopsy and CSF α-syn SAA positivity are summarized in Supplementary Figure 2.

text.text: CSF α-syn SAA results were negative in both patients with MSA, consistent with previous reports in clinically diagnosed patients (12).

text.text: CSF α-syn SAA was negative in 18 of 19 patients with AD or other control diseases (95% specificity).
One patient with AD showed a low-positive SAA result; however, no peripheral Lewy pathology was observed in this case.
Mean F max and AUC were significantly higher in the symptomatic LBD group (Figure 2A, B).
text.formatted: Mean F max and AUC were significantly higher in the symptomatic LBD group (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2A</ref>, <ref type="figure">B</ref>).

text.text: ROC analyses showed AUCs of 1.0 for both indices.
Both mean F max and mean AUC showed perfect separation, with wide cutoff ranges of 2038-7052 RFU and 131-365 RFU × h, respectively.
The mean TTT and T 50 values for positive results were highly correlated (Figure 2C).
text.formatted: The mean TTT and T 50 values for positive results were highly correlated (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2C</ref>).

text.text: Patients with DLB tended to show higher F max and shorter T 50 values than those with PD (with or without MCI/dementia) (Figure 2D).
text.formatted: Patients with DLB tended to show higher F max and shorter T 50 values than those with PD (with or without MCI/dementia) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2D</ref>).

text.text: One patient in the control group with a low positive SAA result at autopsy showed results distinct from those of patients with symptomatic LBD, including a low positivity rate, lower mean F max , and longer T50 (Figure 2D).

text.text: We confirmed the high sensitivity and specificity of CSF α-syn SAA against neuropathological diagnoses of LBD.
Kinetic parameters were also useful for distinguishing characteristics among positive cases.
Previous studies using various SAA methods have reported high specificity (94-98.6%) against pathological diagnoses of LBD (5, (8) (9) (10).
text.formatted: Previous studies using various SAA methods have reported high specificity (94-98.6%) against pathological diagnoses of LBD <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(8)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(9)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(10)</ref>.

text.text: However, most studies assessed Lewy pathology only in the brain, and whether incidental Lewy pathology in the spinal cord or peripheral organs (e.g., sympathetic ganglia) is present in "false-positive" cases remains unknown (10).
text.formatted: However, most studies assessed Lewy pathology only in the brain, and whether incidental Lewy pathology in the spinal cord or peripheral organs (e.g., sympathetic ganglia) is present in "false-positive" cases remains unknown <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(10)</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, we confirmed high specificity (95%) against neuropathological diagnoses using patients with systemic, whole-body assessment of Lewy pathology.
One patient with AD showed a positive CSF α-syn SAA result but lacked Lewy pathology even in the systemic assessment.
Our results indicate that the assay maintains high specificity for LBD and that, in rare cases, low-positive results may occur in individuals without Lewy pathology, even in peripheral organs.
Overall, previous studies have reported high sensitivity of SAA for LBD; however, sensitivity is not perfect and may be lower in certain subtypes, such as patients without hyposmia (13).
text.formatted: Overall, previous studies have reported high sensitivity of SAA for LBD; however, sensitivity is not perfect and may be lower in certain subtypes, such as patients without hyposmia <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(13)</ref>.

text.text: While some SAA-negative patients are later diagnosed with other parkinsonian syndromes, many remain clinically undiagnosed with sporadic PD (14).
text.formatted: While some SAA-negative patients are later diagnosed with other parkinsonian syndromes, many remain clinically undiagnosed with sporadic PD <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(14)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, autopsy validation studies have demonstrated reduced sensitivity when Lewy pathology is limited to the amygdala or brainstem (8) (9) (10) (11).
text.formatted: Moreover, autopsy validation studies have demonstrated reduced sensitivity when Lewy pathology is limited to the amygdala or brainstem <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(8)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(9)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(10)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(11)</ref>.

text.text: In our previous study of clinically diagnosed cases, sensitivity was 88% for DLB and as low as 52% for PD (12).
text.formatted: In our previous study of clinically diagnosed cases, sensitivity was 88% for DLB and as low as 52% for PD <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(12)</ref>.

text.text: Although reduced sensitivity may partly reflect sample handling or the SAA method/interpretation, we found higher sensitivity in patients with abnormal cardiac MIBG findings, suggesting that lower sensitivity was mainly due to a higher proportion of patients with normal cardiac MIBG in the studied population (12).
text.formatted: Although reduced sensitivity may partly reflect sample handling or the SAA method/interpretation, we found higher sensitivity in patients with abnormal cardiac MIBG findings, suggesting that lower sensitivity was mainly due to a higher proportion of patients with normal cardiac MIBG in the studied population <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(12)</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, all patients with LBD with available results showed abnormal cardiac MIBG findings, and we observed a CSF SAA sensitivity of 100% despite some patients being in early disease stages.
Consistent with previous autopsy validation studies, all patients with symptomatic LBD, including those with cognitively normal PD, showed limbic or neocortical Lewy pathology at autopsy.
These findings support the high sensitivity of SAA in patients with LBD with limbic or neocortical involvement, in line with previous studies using different SAA methods.

However, recent studies, including analyses of the BBAR cohort, have shown subsets of patients with relatively greater brain involvement than peripheral involvement, suggesting a brain-first LBD subtype (35, 36).

text.text: In some cases, clinical motor symptoms of PD have been observed in patients with relatively limited Lewy pathology in the amygdala, brainstem, and olfactory bulb (23), or in those without significant cardiac MIBG abnormalities (22).

text.text: Such patients were excluded from both previous and present studies involving antemortem CSF analysis.

Larger studies including these subgroups are needed to determine whether lower CSF α-syn SAA positivity in patients with normal cardiac MIBG (12) is associated with limited Lewy pathology in the brain, as suggested in patients without motor symptoms (8) (9) (10).

text.text: Previous studies have shown patients with limited peripheral pathology, suggesting a body-first subtype of LBD (35).
text.formatted: Previous studies have shown patients with limited peripheral pathology, suggesting a body-first subtype of LBD <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(35)</ref>.

text.text: A recent study further suggested that these patients can be subdivided into sympathetic and parasympathetic subtypes (36).

text.text: Whether CSF α-syn SAA becomes positive in such patients remains unclear (11).

text.text: Previous studies have shown that SAA can become positive in the premotor phase, including in individuals with isolated REM sleep behavior disorder, hyposmia, and pure autonomic failure (11, 13).

text.text: In this pilot study, no patients with limited whole-body Lewy pathology were identified.
Larger studies are warranted to identify the pathological threshold at which SAA becomes positive.
Kinetic parameters provided valuable insights into differences among SAA-positive patients, as previously reported.
Patients with DLB showed higher mean F max and shorter mean T 50 values.
These findings align with previous studies using different SAA methods, which reported associations with cognitive decline (37) (38) (39).

text.text: Notably, one control patient without Lewy pathology (false-positive) showed increased fluorescence above the predetermined threshold; however, the positivity rate and mean F max were lower, and T 50 was longer than in patients with symptomatic LBD.
Previous studies have suggested that incorporating kinetic parameters can improve diagnostic accuracy (34), although criteria are required given different methodologies.
text.formatted: Previous studies have suggested that incorporating kinetic parameters can improve diagnostic accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(34)</ref>, although criteria are required given different methodologies.

text.text: Nevertheless, confirming the absence of Lewy pathology in the peripheral organs would be important to accurately determine "false-positive" cases for generation of such criteria.

While Lewy pathology was prevalent in the olfactory bulb (24), sympathetic ganglia (22, 25), spinal cord (26), esophagus (23), and heart (22, 25), the positivity was as low as 25% in the skin in this study.

text.text: We previously reported that Lewy pathology can be detected in the skin in patients with LBD (27), and the positivity rate was approximately 50% by examining one region and was higher by examining two skin regions (27).

text.text: A recent multicenter study reported even higher positivity rates using antemortem samples from multiple skin regions (40).

text.text: Although our results may suggest that CSF α-syn SAA is more sensitive than pathological examination of the skin, direct comparison using antemortem samples from multiple skin regions is necessary to clarify this point.
Our assay used in this study was negative in patients with MSA as previously reported (12).

text.text: Although MSA is characterized by widespread α-syn aggregates, the structures of the α-syn filaments are different from those in LBD (41).
text.formatted: Although MSA is characterized by widespread α-syn aggregates, the structures of the α-syn filaments are different from those in LBD <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(41)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, previous studies have reported lower sensitivity of CSF α-syn SAA in MSA (4).

Newer assays optimized to detect MSA have higher sensitivity than previous assays and discriminate between LBD and MSA by different assay characteristics, including lower F max and shorter T 50 values in MSA (34, 42, 43).

text.text: Further optimization is needed for our assay to detect CSF α-syn SAA positivity in patients with MSA.
The strength of this study is the detailed, systemic whole-body assessment of Lewy pathology in a community-based cohort.
Limitations include the small sample size, lack of patients with LBD limited to either the brain or peripheral organs, and the use of a single in-house SAA method, precluding robust conclusions.
Larger studies using different SAA methodologies in autopsy cohorts with systemic Lewy pathology assessment are warranted for a better understanding of biomarker-based diagnosis in LBD.
